questions.question: Investigators seize a laptop that may be evidence in a fraud case. Each handoff is documented: who took it, when, where it was stored, who opened the evidence bag, what was extracted, and who returned it. The signed log is admissible in court because it proves the evidence was never altered or substituted. Which IR construct is this?
options: Chain of custody
User activity monitoring — records OS-level file accesses, not evidence handling
ITSM ticket workflow — tracks alert triage, not legal evidence handling
Patch-management change record — documents patching, not evidence custody
questions.explanation: Chain of custody documents: who collected evidence, when, where, how, storage conditions, and every person who had access. Hash values verify integrity. Breaks in chain of custody can make evidence inadmissible in court.

questions.question: A SaaS startup wants users to grant a third-party app limited, scoped access to their account (e.g., 'read my calendar, do not send email') without ever sharing their password with the third-party app. The mechanism must support short-lived access tokens, refresh tokens, and scope strings. Which standard fits?
options: PBKDF2, a key-derivation function used to slow password cracking by iterating a hash — PBKDF2 outputs a derived key, not bearer tokens used in an authorisation-delegation flow
OAuth 2.0, an authorisation-delegation protocol with bearer tokens
SAML 2.0, an SSO assertion exchange between identity and service providers
Mutual TLS, in which client and server present X.509 certificates to each other
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 lets a resource owner authorise a third-party client to receive a scoped, short-lived access token (plus an optional refresh token) — the client never sees the user's password. PBKDF2 is a hash function, not a protocol. SAML is for federated SSO between IdP and SP, not third-party delegation. mTLS authenticates services to each other, with no end-user delegation step.

questions.question: A 24×7 team works from a room full of dashboards. Their job is to ingest alerts from EDR, SIEM, and cloud trails, triage them, run playbook investigations, escalate when a real attack is found, and hand off to engineering for remediation. They do NOT run physical security or compliance audits. Which team is this?
options: Data-centre operations responsible for racks, power, and cooling
The physical security team managing guards, badges, and CCTV
A Security Operations Centre handling detection and incident response
Governance and compliance team running audits and producing reports
questions.explanation: A SOC ingests detection signals from EDR/SIEM/cloud trails, triages, investigates, and drives incident response — the exact list of duties given. Physical security and governance/compliance are distinct functions in any large security organisation. Data-centre operations runs the underlying facility, not the alert pipeline.

questions.question: An organization's outbound mail is being marked as spam by recipients and a phishing campaign is impersonating the company's domain. The security team wants to publish authoritative records that let receiving mail servers (1) verify the sending IP is authorised, (2) confirm the message wasn't altered in transit using a cryptographic signature, and (3) decide what to do (quarantine/reject) when checks fail. Which combination of standards meets all three needs?
options: S/MIME and PGP — both provide end-to-end message body encryption between mailboxes
TLS, STARTTLS, and MTA-STS — encrypt the transport channel between mail servers
SPF + DKIM + DMARC — authorise sender IPs, sign messages, and define a failure policy
Anti-virus, attachment sandboxing, and URL rewriting — inspect content for malicious payloads
questions.explanation: Email authentication trio: SPF (which IPs can send for domain), DKIM (signature proving message integrity), DMARC (policy: if SPF and DKIM both fail, quarantine or reject). Essential for preventing phishing via domain impersonation.

questions.question: An OT environment has a small, fixed inventory of trusted engineering applications. The security team wants to allow ONLY those binaries to execute on production hosts — every other process (new utility, malware, lateral-movement tool) must be blocked by default. The deny-by-default decision is made at the OS, not by signature databases. Which control is being described?
options: Application allowlisting enforced by the host operating system
Signature-based antivirus that blocks executables matching known-bad hashes
An IP blocklist applied at the perimeter firewall against threat-intel feeds
An MDM app-store category filter that restricts which marketplaces are usable
questions.explanation: Application allowlisting (Windows Defender Application Control, AppLocker, Carbon Black App Control) enforces deny-by-default at the OS — only approved binaries run. This is the strongest endpoint posture for environments with a stable software inventory, especially OT. Signature AV is allow-by-default with a known-bad list. IP blocklists filter network traffic, not process execution. MDM filters marketplaces, not arbitrary binaries.

questions.question: A payments processor must meet PCI-DSS key-management requirements: the master encryption key for cardholder data must (1) be generated inside tamper-resistant hardware, (2) NEVER leave that hardware in plaintext, and (3) sign/encrypt operations are performed by sending data INTO the device. Which device category satisfies all three requirements?
options: USB encrypted thumb-drive hardware — a tamper-resistant device for files, not for non-exportable keys
Hardware Security Module (HSM) — a tamper-resistant device that generates and uses keys in-place
Software cryptographic library — runs on commodity hardware, not a tamper-resistant key device
Network firewall hardware — a perimeter device, tamper-resistant chassis but not a key-custody device
questions.explanation: An HSM is a tamper-resistant, FIPS-140-validated device whose private keys are non-exportable; applications send data IN and get signed/encrypted output back. USB drives store data, not non-exportable keys. Software libraries hold keys in process memory. A firewall is perimeter security, unrelated to key custody. NOTE: prior version of this question had the wrong correct-answer index (described a firewall appliance as the HSM definition) — fixed during the 2026-05-13 audit pass.

questions.question: An HR director receives an email that uses her first name, references the cloud-migration project from last week's all-hands, mentions the CFO by name, and asks her to wire $42 000 to a 'new vendor' urgently. The email's reply-to is a look-alike domain registered yesterday. The lure is highly customised to her role and the current company context. Which attack class is this?
options: Generic phishing — mass-mailed lure with no personal customisation
Vishing — voice-channel social engineering, no email lure
Spear phishing
USB-drop pretexting — physical-media lure, not an email
questions.explanation: Spear phishing success rate >> mass phishing because it's personalized. Attacker researches target on LinkedIn, company website, social media. Then crafts an email from 'their CEO' or 'IT helpdesk' about something plausible. High-value targets: executives, finance, IT admins.

questions.question: A multi-cloud enterprise wants a single control plane to: (1) discover unsanctioned SaaS usage (shadow IT) from corporate networks, (2) apply DLP and encryption policies to data flowing INTO sanctioned cloud apps, and (3) sit between users and providers so the policy applies regardless of endpoint. Which control category fits all three?
options: Cloud-native firewall — controls VPC packets, not user-to-SaaS flows
Cloud identity provider — federates user auth, no DLP or shadow-IT discovery
API gateway — rate-limits user API calls, not a SaaS policy point
CASB
questions.explanation: CASBs (Netskope, McAfee MVISION, Microsoft CASB) discover what cloud apps employees use (shadow IT), enforce policies (block sensitive data uploads to personal Dropbox), detect risky behavior, and provide compliance controls for cloud usage.

questions.question: A CISO is replacing legacy signature-only AV on 4 000 endpoints. They want a control that (1) continuously collects telemetry (process exec, registry, network) from each endpoint, (2) applies behavioural analytics on the central console to detect attacks signature AV would miss, and (3) gives the analyst a remote shell / kill / quarantine response action from the console. Which control category is being described?
options: EDR — endpoint detection and response, continuous telemetry + behavioural detection + remote response
Traditional antivirus — signature scans of files on a schedule, no behavioural detection on endpoint telemetry
Network IDS — inspects packets in transit, no endpoint-process telemetry or remote response
SIEM — aggregates and correlates logs, but does not execute response actions on the endpoint
questions.explanation: EDR (CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) records all endpoint activity (process creation, network connections, file changes), uses ML/behavioral analysis to detect threats, and enables forensic investigation.

questions.question: A development team needs to store user passwords. They considered three primitives. Senior engineering insists on the primitive that: produces a fixed-length output regardless of input size, can't be reversed back to the password, makes a one-bit change in the input produce a completely different output, and makes it computationally infeasible to find two inputs with the same output. Which primitive is being described?
options: A symmetric block cipher in CBC mode — produces reversible ciphertext output, not what's needed
A cryptographic hash function
An asymmetric key-exchange like Diffie–Hellman — output is a shared secret, not a password digest
A MAC such as HMAC — output authenticates a message but requires holding a shared secret key
questions.explanation: Hash functions (SHA-256, SHA-3, MD5 [broken]): file integrity checking, password storage, digital signatures, blockchain. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken (collision attacks demonstrated). Use SHA-256 or SHA-3 for security-sensitive applications. Required properties: deterministic, one-way (can't reverse), collision-resistant (different inputs → different outputs), avalanche effect (small input change → completely different output)

questions.question: A bank's security architecture deliberately layers controls: TLS at the edge, WAF in front of the app, network segmentation between tiers, IPS in the DMZ, MFA on every privileged login, FDE on laptops. The CISO explains the design intent: if any single control is bypassed, the next layer should still contain the attacker. Which security principle is this?
options: Deep Packet Inspection — a capability of some controls, not a layered architecture principle
Perimeter-only defence — concentrates controls at the edge, opposite of the principle described
Defence in depth — overlapping layered controls so one bypass does not compromise the whole
Single point of inspection — one NGFW carries all controls; opposite of layered controls
questions.explanation: Defense in depth (Swiss cheese model): multiple imperfect controls whose holes don't overlap. Examples: perimeter firewall + network segmentation + host firewall + EDR + SIEM + user training. Attacker must defeat multiple controls.

questions.question: A security architect is reviewing a new access-control component. They insist on a specific default behaviour: if the policy engine cannot reach the directory or the decision is ambiguous, the request must be DENIED rather than allowed. Production engineers worry about availability impact; security holds the line. Which design principle is being applied?
options: Fail-open — default to allow on failure to preserve service availability over secure default
Fail-safe defaults — default to deny on failure or ambiguity, a secure-by-default posture
Defense in depth — overlap multiple defaults so one component failure does not expose the resource
Least privilege — each subject gets the minimum default permissions needed to do its job
questions.explanation: Fail-safe defaults: new accounts get no permissions (least privilege from day 1), firewall default-deny, locks fail-closed (secure mode) not fail-open. Failure modes should preserve security over availability in most cases.

questions.question: Threat-intel analysts find that a niche industry-association website used daily by employees of three target defence contractors was silently compromised three weeks ago to serve a browser exploit ONLY to visitors arriving from those three companies' IP ranges. Other visitors saw the normal site. Which attack pattern fits the evidence?
options: Watering-hole attack — adversary poisons a site routinely visited by the target and serves payloads only to matching visitors

Critical-infrastructure compromise — adversary attacks a SCADA control system target site directly, not a web site frequented by the target group; end-users are not visitors to an exploited third-party web page
Software supply-chain attack — adversary targets an upstream library, not the target audience's daily site
SQL injection — adversary attacks a website's database; the target's visiting browsers are not the focus
questions.explanation: Watering hole attacks target specific industries: compromise the popular security blog that all security professionals read, or the car parts forum. Victims visit trusted sites, get infected. Hard to prevent with URL filtering alone.

questions.question: During the DESIGN phase of a new payment service, the architect enumerates: which assets need protection, what an attacker could do (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, DoS, Elevation of privilege), and which controls mitigate each. The output drives the design before any code is written. Which structured activity is this?
options: Malware family classification — categorises samples post-hoc, not design-time analysis
Threat modelling using STRIDE — design-time identification of threats per asset/component
Open-vulnerability risk score — measures running systems, not designs
Red-team attack planning — execution-time adversary simulation, after the design
questions.explanation: Threat modelling is a design-time activity. STRIDE (Spoofing/Tampering/Repudiation/Information Disclosure/DoS/Elevation of Privilege) is one canonical methodology. PASTA and LINDDUN are others. NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index (marked red-team planning as the threat-modelling definition) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A remote employee connects to the corporate VPN from an airport's public Wi-Fi. VPN split tunneling is enabled: work application traffic routes through the encrypted corporate tunnel while streaming and personal browsing go directly to the internet. A security analyst flags this configuration during a quarterly review. What is the PRIMARY security concern?
options: All VPN tunnel traffic is visible to the airport Wi-Fi operator because split tunneling disables encryption for connections routed through the corporate tunnel
A compromised endpoint on the local wireless network could reach internal resources by pivoting through the active corporate tunnel
Corporate bandwidth is wasted because all personal streaming traffic is forced through the VPN gateway before reaching content-delivery networks
Split tunneling prevents the corporate DLP solution from inspecting outbound personal traffic, creating a data-exfiltration blind spot for the security team
questions.explanation: Split tunneling means the endpoint is simultaneously attached to an open local network (where rogue access points or malicious devices may exist) and the corporate VPN tunnel; malware or an attacker who compromises the device locally can traverse that tunnel directly into corporate systems. Option C is factually wrong — split tunneling reduces traffic flowing through the corporate VPN gateway, not increases it.

questions.question: An organisation new to security wants a vendor-neutral, voluntary framework that organises security activities into a small set of top-level functions for board-level reporting. The framework should NOT be a mandatory compliance regime, NOT issue certifications to companies, and NOT prescribe an incident-response template. Which framework fits these requirements?
options: PCI-DSS framework — mandatory, prescriptive controls grouped into compliance requirements
FedRAMP framework — mandatory for US-gov cloud, organised into authorisation baselines
NIST Cybersecurity Framework
ISO 27001 framework — certifiable management-system standard, organised into Annex A controls
questions.explanation: NIST CSF: Identify (asset inventory, risk assessment), Protect (access control, training, hardening), Detect (monitoring, anomaly detection), Respond (incident response), Recover (recovery planning). Widely adopted for structuring security programs.

questions.question: A company is moving from a traditional perimeter-based model to a Zero Trust Architecture. Which principle BEST captures the core philosophy the security team should adopt?
options: Never trust, always verify — authenticate and authorize every request regardless of network location
Trust internal subnets implicitly and apply rigorous inspection only to ingress traffic at the edge firewall
Allow all east-west data center traffic by default, blocking only connections to known-malicious external IPs
Replace per-request MFA with session-scoped single sign-on so each user authenticates only once per workday
questions.explanation: Zero Trust assumes the network is hostile and no user, device, or workload is trusted by default — every access request is authenticated, authorized, and continuously evaluated. Identity becomes the new perimeter, and micro-segmentation prevents lateral movement.

questions.question: A global enterprise wants to consolidate SD-WAN, ZTNA, secure web gateway, CASB, and FWaaS into a single cloud-delivered service to support its remote workforce. Which model should the architect propose?
options: A DLP overlay on the existing MPLS backbone — adds data-loss-prevention to a fixed-line WAN but does not provide cloud-native secure access for remote workers or branch offices without hair-pinning traffic
A SASE platform (Secure Access Service Edge)
An on-premises NGFW cluster with VPN concentrators
A hub-and-spoke VPN with split tunneling
questions.explanation: SASE converges networking (SD-WAN) and security (ZTNA, SWG, CASB, FWaaS) into a single cloud-delivered service, applied close to the user. It fits distributed/remote workforces better than backhauling traffic to a central data center.

questions.question: A SOC manager wants visibility that correlates telemetry from endpoints, network traffic, cloud workloads, and email security in a single platform. The current EDR only covers laptops and servers. Which solution BEST addresses the gap?
options: Deploy a second EDR vendor in parallel to fill endpoint telemetry gaps — adding a second EDR does not deliver a unified cross-domain solution integrating cloud workload, email security, and network visibility
Replace the SIEM with a plain log aggregator storing raw events without correlation or alerting capabilities
Migrate to an XDR solution for unified detection spanning endpoint, network, cloud, and email telemetry
Add a host-based IPS to every endpoint to block known-bad signatures at the OS layer
questions.explanation: EDR is endpoint-scoped. XDR (Extended Detection and Response) correlates signals across endpoint, network, cloud, identity, and email, reducing alert silos and surfacing multi-vector attacks. It typically replaces or augments EDR with broader telemetry.

questions.question: A security team forms a dedicated unit that proactively searches the environment for hidden adversarial activity that automated tools have not flagged. Analysts follow hunts derived from threat-intelligence and hypothesis, not automated alerts. Which activity is this?
options: Automated vulnerability scanning — discovers software weaknesses by probing assets with known signatures rather than proactively seeking evidence of active threat actor behaviour within the environment
Penetration testing
Red teaming
Threat hunting
questions.explanation: Threat hunting is a proactive, hypothesis-driven activity that assumes a breach has already occurred and searches for dwelling threats using TTPs and IOCs. Unlike alert-driven SOC work, hunters look for what existing detections may have missed.

questions.question: A facilities team is deploying hundreds of IoT sensors (HVAC, lighting, badge readers) across a smart office building. Which combination of controls BEST hardens the deployment against common IoT compromise?
options: Place IoT devices on a dedicated VLAN, change default credentials, and apply firmware updates on a managed schedule
Allow IoT devices on the corporate user VLAN so help desk staff can reach them for support without extra config
Delegate all security to the vendor's cloud portal and disable local logging to reduce device resource consumption
Expose device management ports to the internet via port forwarding to enable remote maintenance by the vendor
questions.explanation: IoT hardening fundamentals: network segmentation (dedicated VLAN/subnet to limit blast radius), changing default credentials (Mirai-style botnets exploit them), and patching firmware on a schedule. Flat networks and exposed management ports are the leading IoT attack vectors. change default credentials, and apply firmware updates on a managed schedule

questions.question: A mobile banking app must resist man-in-the-middle attacks even when an attacker has installed a rogue root CA on the device. Which control BEST protects the TLS connection between the app and the bank's API?
options: Enforcing TLS 1.3 with strong forward-secret cipher suites on every API endpoint
Certificate pinning — client matches against a pre-configured key only, rejecting all other CAs
Using OAuth 2.0 scoped access tokens to authorize every API call from the mobile client
Enabling HSTS on the API endpoint to force clients to upgrade all connections to HTTPS
questions.explanation: Certificate pinning hardcodes the expected server certificate or public key inside the app, so any other cert (even one signed by a trusted CA) is rejected. This defeats MITM attacks that rely on installing rogue root CAs on the device. TLS version and HSTS still rely on trusted CA chains.

questions.question: A development team wants to test their running web application for vulnerabilities like injection and broken authentication by sending real HTTP requests against the deployed staging environment. Which testing approach are they using?
options: DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing)
SCA (Software Composition Analysis)
IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing)
SAST (Static Application Security Testing)
questions.explanation: DAST tests a running application from the outside by sending crafted HTTP requests, mimicking an attacker. SAST analyzes source code without execution; IAST instruments the app to combine runtime and code analysis; SCA inspects third-party dependencies for known CVEs.

questions.question: A SaaS platform needs to let third-party apps access a user's calendar data on their behalf without sharing the user's password. Which protocol is the BEST fit, and why?
options: SAML 2.0, because it issues XML-based assertions for cross-domain single sign-on federation
Kerberos, because it uses ticket-granting tickets for mutual authentication inside a Kerberos realm
RADIUS, because it centralizes AAA for network device and VPN access control
OAuth 2.0, because it is an authorization framework that issues scoped access tokens for delegated access
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework: the user grants a third-party app a scoped access token without sharing credentials. SAML is for federated authentication/SSO between identity and service providers — a different problem. Kerberos and RADIUS are not designed for delegated cloud-app access.

questions.question: A CISO discovers that employees across multiple departments are using unsanctioned cloud file-sharing services to collaborate, bypassing the approved platform. Which control will BEST discover these shadow IT services and enforce governance over them?
options: Deploy a CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) to discover, monitor, and apply policy to cloud app usage — a CASB provides visibility and control but does not require employees to authenticate through the corporate identity provider before accessing apps
Block all outbound HTTPS traffic at the perimeter firewall to prevent access to any unapproved cloud service
Send a company-wide email reminding staff to use the approved platform and outlining disciplinary consequences
Require MFA on the corporate identity provider so employees authenticate before accessing any cloud application
questions.explanation: A CASB sits between users and cloud services and provides shadow-IT discovery (from proxy/firewall logs), data security, threat protection, and compliance for both sanctioned and unsanctioned SaaS. Blocking all HTTPS is impractical, and MFA does not address discovery. monitor, and apply policy to sanctioned and unsanctioned cloud apps

questions.question: A government agency is concerned that an adversary is intercepting and storing today's TLS-encrypted traffic to decrypt later once large-scale quantum computers exist. Which strategy BEST mitigates this 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat?
options: Rotate RSA-2048 certificates every 30 days to minimize the window during which captured ciphertexts remain exploitable by future quantum systems
Begin migrating to NIST post-quantum cryptography standards such as CRYSTALS-Kyber for key encapsulation and CRYSTALS-Dilithium for signatures
Increase AES symmetric key length from 128 to 256 bits while retaining the existing classical RSA key exchange mechanism unchanged
Disable Perfect Forward Secrecy to simplify key management and reduce TLS handshake computational overhead on servers
questions.explanation: Harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks target asymmetric algorithms (RSA, ECC) that quantum computers will eventually break. NIST has standardized post-quantum algorithms — CRYSTALS-Kyber (KEM) and CRYSTALS-Dilithium (signatures) — and organizations protecting long-lived secrets should plan a PQC migration now.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are characteristics of a TPM (Trusted Platform Module) that distinguish it from an HSM (Hardware Security Module)?
options: Soldered to the motherboard of a single host
Network-attached, shared across many servers
Designed primarily for full-disk-encryption key sealing and platform attestation
Designed primarily for high-throughput cryptographic operations in PKI infrastructure
questions.explanation: A TPM is a chip soldered onto the motherboard of one host, used for measured boot, attestation, and sealing keys (notably BitLocker FVEK). An HSM is typically a network-attached or PCIe device built for high-throughput crypto — used by CAs, payment processors, etc. The other two options describe an HSM.

questions.question: A pentester is told to use ONLY passive reconnaissance against a target. Which TWO activities are still allowed?
options: Running an Nmap SYN scan against the target's public IPs
Querying public WHOIS and DNS records
Searching Shodan and Google for indexed pages of the target
Sending a crafted HTTP request to test for SQL injection
questions.explanation: Passive recon = no packet sent directly to the target. WHOIS/DNS queries hit registries, not the target. Shodan/Google searches use third-party caches. A SYN scan and an HTTP probe both touch the target, making them active recon.
